At the body temperatures typical of active foraging periods in this species (40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]), the basal metabolic rate of the Tyrannine woodcreeper (Dendrocincla tyrannina) has been measured at 96.36 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 96.36 milliliters of oxygen per hour], a value that aligns with predictions for a bird of its size in the suboscine passerine lineage. The eggs of this species, which are incubated for roughly 25 days [ab = roughly 25 days] at an average nest temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C], are relatively large, measuring 35.2 millimeters in length and 27.7 millimeters in width. Based on these egg dimensions, the calculated initial wet weight of the hatchling is about 14.4 grams [Ww0 = about 14.4 grams], a mass that is typical for a neotropical furnariid emerging from such an egg.

After hatching, the altricial nestling undergoes a rapid but steady period of mass gain, reaching a wet weight of 16 grams  by just five days post-hatch. This represents a modest increase from the hatchling mass, reflecting the early phase of skeletal and muscular development before the exponential growth associated with feather production begins. The chick is initially brooded almost constantly by the female, with the male providing the majority of the food during the first week. Published growth curves for congeners suggest that this rate of mass accumulation is consistent with a life history strategy prioritizing rapid development of the digestive and thermoregulatory systems over immediate structural size increase, a critical adaptation for the cool, high-altitude cloud forest habitats this species occupies.

Under the thermal conditions typical of brooding (40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]), fledging occurs at 29 days after hatching [tx = 29 days after hatching], marking the end of the nestling phase. Following fledging, the young bird enters a juvenile phase where it remains dependent on its parents for food for several weeks. Sexual maturation, or the onset of puberty, is reached at 87 days after hatching [tp = 87 days after hatching] at this same body temperature, a timeline that is relatively rapid for a bird of this size at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This accelerates the potential for the young-of-the-year to participate in the following breeding season, though in practice, many first-year birds may not successfully establish a territory.

The timing of the first successful reproductive event, or the age at first brood, occurs considerably later than the attainment of physical maturity. The time since birth at first brood is approximately 474.5 days [tR = approximately 474.5 days], when measured under the same standard metabolic temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This substantial delay between puberty and first reproduction is a common pattern among tropical passerines, where competition for high-quality territories and the slow pace of learning efficient foraging techniques in a stable environment often defer the onset of breeding. In terms of annual reproductive output, this species produces a single clutch of two eggs per breeding attempt, with a maximum frequency of approximately one to two broods per year, resulting in a maximum daily reproduction rate that is best expressed through the combination of a clutch size of 2 eggs per nest [N_R_i = 2 eggs per nest] and a maximum of 2 breeding attempts per year [F_R_i = 2 breeding attempts per year].

The ultimate wet weight for adult females of Dendrocincla tyrannina stabilizes at approximately 54.9 grams [Wwi = approximately 54.9 grams], falling near the middle of the reported body mass range of 40 to 64 grams for this species. Males tend to be slightly heavier than females, although the difference is often less than 5 grams and is rarely significant in small sample sizes. In terms of longevity, the maximum lifespan recorded for this species in the wild is approximately 10.7 years [am = approximately 10.7 years] under the standard metabolic temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], a figure consistent with the high adult survival rates documented for tropical insectivorous passerines that exhibit a slow pace of life. The species relies on its strong, slightly decurved bill to flake bark and probe epiphytic moss for arthropods, a foraging niche that requires considerable skill to exploit efficiently.
